items.title: Multivalent antiviral conjugates enhance activity against Influenza via cross-linking viruses
items.summary: Nature Communications, Published online: 04 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78126-3 A multivalent antiviral conjugates (AVCs) platform was established by conjugating NA inhibitors and Fc domain. AVCs cross-link flu viruses, blocking entry and release. Trivalent peramivir-Fc conjugate outperformed clinical drugs in mice.

items.title: A family of small proteins links c-di-GMP riboswitch signaling with sporulation in Clostridioides difficile
items.summary: Nature Communications, Published online: 04 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78452-6 The second messenger c-di-GMP inhibits sporulation in the pathogenic bacterium Clostridioides difficile through unclear mechanisms. Here, Badilla Lobo et al. show that the expression of sporulation genes is modulated by a family of small membrane-associated proteins encoded by genes that are controlled by c-diGMP-regulated riboswitches.

items.title: A CCL21 gene-modified dendritic cell vaccine combined with pembrolizumab in advanced non-small cell lung cancer: a phase I trial
items.summary: Nature Communications, Published online: 04 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78130-7 Feasibility and safety profile of intratumoral administration of a DC vaccine overexpressing CCL21 (CCL21-DC) have been previously reported in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Here the authors report safety, clinical outcomes and immunological correlates of a phase I trial of CCL21-DC in combination with anti-PD1 pembrolizumab in patients with advanced NSCLC.

items.title: Volitional control of wearable robots
items.summary: Nature Communications, Published online: 03 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78416-w This Comment motivates the development of human–machine interfaces that decode spinal motor neuron activity and resulting muscle force information in moving humans. Such interfaces could enable users across the neuromuscular functional spectrum to volitionally control wearable robots with muscle-like behaviour.

items.title: Thermally programmed disassembly and reconstruction of 2D polymer platelets via melting-governed crystallization-driven self-assembly
items.summary: Nature Communications, Published online: 03 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-77973-4 ‘Crystallization-driven self-assembly is a useful tool for the synthesis of polymer nanostructures with precise dimensions, but the melting behavior of polymer crystals grown in solution has remained largely unexplored. Here, the authors show that melting temperature is a structurally sensitive descriptor and an active design parameter for 2D platelets.’

items.title: Sustainability cost of defect engineering in color centers for quantum communications
items.summary: Nature Communications, Published online: 03 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78261-x Sustainable manufacturing is becoming an increasingly important consideration for emerging quantum technologies. Here, the authors assess the environmental, chemical, human-health, and economic impacts of defect engineering strategies for color-center platforms used in quantum communications, highlighting trade-offs between quantum functionality and resource demands while identifying lower-impact solutions.

items.title: Bulk mesophases modeling of ferroelectric nematic liquid crystals
items.summary: Nature Communications, Published online: 03 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78039-1 Ferroelectric nematic liquid crystals are an emerging class of materials in which nematic orientational order coexists with spontaneous macroscopic polarization. Vats et al. develop a free-energy framework to rationalize their bulk structures and predict potential bend-instability-driven mesophases.

items.title: Near-atomistic simulations reveal the molecular principles that control chromatin structure and phase separation
items.summary: Nature Communications, Published online: 03 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78050-6 Russell et al. introduce a 10 × faster, chemically detailed chromatin model bridging molecular and genomic scales, revealing how DNA sequence, spacing and histone acetylation govern chromatin folding and phase separation.

The authors use magneto-optical birefringence imaging to show that a Pt capping layer enables ultrafast laser pulses to modify domains in insulating NiO and CoO films. Wrachtrup SiC-based quantum magnetometry is vital for advanced sensing fields because it offers a path to volume-compatible chips, but it is held back because its sensitivity is lower than other platforms like N- V diamond color centers. This study uses a planar 4 H -SiC waveguide platform and wafer-scale fabrication to seamlessly integrate and excite large V2 ensembles. Notably, this streamlined layout achieves a shot-noise limit of 30 nT/√Hz, boosting sensitivity by 2–3 orders of magnitude over that of standard, confocal SiC methods while preserving coherent control.

items.title: The timescale of forming Earth’s earliest water ocean in the Hadean Eon
items.summary: Abstract The timing of the first water ocean formation on Earth is critical for understanding the onset of habitability, but the duration of this process remains poorly constrained. Using a heat-budget model for the early atmosphere-ocean system, this study quantifies the transition from the final solidification of the magma ocean to the establishment of a stable hydrosphere. The results demonstrate that once the mantle transitioned to solid-state convection, a thick primordial steam atmosphere can radiatively cool and condense into a global water ocean within 10,000 years. Sensitivity tests indicate that this rapid condensation timescale is robust across reasonably oxidized volatile scenarios, even when accounting for cloud feedback and alternative mantle rheological trajectories. This finding suggests that a stable hydrosphere emerged almost contemporaneously with the solidification of Earth’s earliest crust, and provides a physical framework for the existence of liquid water by ∼4.4 Ga on the Earth and other terrestrial planets.

items.title: Colloquium: Laboratory exploration of planetary interiors
authors: G. W. Collins, S. Seager, J. Eggert, X. Gong, M. Huff, J. R. Rygg, T.-A. Suer, and R. Jeanloz
items.summary: W. Collins, S. Seager, J. Eggert, X. Gong, M. Huff, J. R. Rygg, T.-A. Suer, and R. Jeanloz Astronomers observe thousands of planets beyond our Solar System, many with extreme interior conditions. Deep inside these worlds, gravity produces pressures millions to billions of times stronger than Earth’s atmosphere. At these pressures, matter behaves in surprising ways: hydrogen can become metallic, water and ammonia may form exotic superionic states, and hydrocarbons can turn into diamond. This Colloquium describes how studying these unusual materials helps scientists explain how planets form, evolve, and generate magnetic fields and magma oceans. Using powerful lasers and pulsed-power facilities, researchers recreate such pressures in laboratories, revealing new physics and improving understanding of the hidden interiors of distant planets.

items.title: Satellite evidence of unequal basin-scale recovery from severe droughts
items.summary: Abstract Severe droughts deplete terrestrial water storage, jeopardizing ecosystems and human well-being. Yet, the pace and extent to which large river basins recover from such events remain unknown at the global scale. Here, integrating GRACE/FO water storage observations with state-of-the-art water availability estimates, we disentangle hydrological recovery following 468 basin-scale severe droughts with discernible impacts globally from 2003 to 2025. Recovery to pre-drought conditions is widespread but uneven across basins and events, with persistent deficits disproportionately concentrated in drylands or endorheic basins. Where recovery occurs, trajectories are highly variable and nonlinear, ranging from rapid and steady recovery to delayed responses. These dynamics are strongly modulated by post-drought water availability, while persistent deficits are further associated with recurrent severe droughts and intensive human water use. Our findings reveal global inequalities in drought recovery and underscore the need for region-specific strategies to manage water scarcity under accelerating climate change and rising water demand.

items.summary: Producing narrow-band, high-spectral-density pulses from an x-ray free-electron laser (XFEL) is important for demanding applications at extreme photon energies, such as high-resolution spectroscopy and studies of structural dynamics, but conventional hard-x-ray self-seeding becomes increasingly limited as photon energy increases. This study extends hard-x-ray self-seeding at the European XFEL to 18 keV, and explores second-harmonic-generation self-seeding as a route toward even higher photon energies. Experiments demonstrate coherent amplification of the second harmonic at 15 and 18 keV, while simulations show the potential for narrowband operation at 30 keV.

Each rung of this hierarchy yielded new insight and specific predictions, not just for global warming but also for the spatial patterns of warming—predictions borne out by subsequent observations.

Kemppinen Arrays of Josephson junctions can generate highly accurate voltage waveforms at cryogenic temperatures, and when optically driven are promising for low-dissipation control of superconducting quantum circuits. Their use in quantum computing has been limited, though, by the frequency at which control data can be delivered to the arrays. Combining externally shunted junctions of high characteristic frequency and low critical current, fast optical pulses, and a high-bandwidth photodiode, this study demonstrates data transfer at frequencies up to 60 GHz, about four times as high as usual for Josephson arbitrary-waveform synthesizers—and even higher frequencies may be attainable.

items.title: Quantum geometry phenomena in condensed matter systems

items.summary: The observation by Berry that adiabatic transport around a closed loop leads to a phase in addition to that determined by the energy spectrum lies at the heart of topology in solids. Such geometrical effects have measurable physical consequences, notably quantum Hall physics in the absence of an external magnetic field—all of which are encapsulated by the quantum geometric tensor. The imaginary part of this tensor is the Berry curvature, and the real part encodes the distance between nearby wave functions and hence is referred to as the quantum metric. In recent years, the quantum geometric tensor has proven central to novel many-body effects in quantum matter, including superconductivity in flat-band systems, third-order nonlinear Hall effects, and second-harmonic nonlinear Hall effects, to name a few. This review catalogs these advances with an eye toward showing how new many-body effects arise from quantum geometry.
